name: Curriculum and Learning Outcomes
title: Curriculum and Learning Outcomes
answer: Curriculum and learning outcomes covers the design of a course as a sequence of intended capabilities, and the evidence that students actually reach them. It sits inside course design and teaching, where a syllabus is treated as a plan for learning rather than a list of topics to be covered. The scope runs from writing programme-level outcomes down to the week-by-week activities and assessments that produce them. It also covers the feedback loop, since outcomes are only meaningful if they are measured and the measurement feeds back into the next version of the course.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Curriculum and learning outcomes covers the design of a course as a sequence of intended capabilities, and the evidence that students actually reach them. It sits inside course design and teaching, where a syllabus is treated as a plan for learning rather than a list of topics to be covered. The scope runs from writing programme-level outcomes down to the week-by-week activities and assessments that produce them. It also covers the feedback loop, since outcomes are only meaningful if they are measured and the measurement feeds back into the next version of the course.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a learning management system for delivery and grades, a document store for syllabi, rubrics and accreditation records, and whatever assessment tools the institution already supports. Version control or a shared drive matters more than people expect, because a curriculum is revised across terms and the history of those revisions is the record. Nothing here requires specialist machine learning infrastructure, though analytics from the learning management system are often used to check whether outcomes are being met. The real constraint is usually institutional process, not software.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Design typically starts from outcomes written as observable verbs, then works backwards to assessments that can demonstrate them and forwards to the activities that prepare students for those assessments. Alignment between the three is the central discipline, and a rubric is the usual instrument that makes the alignment checkable. Instructors gather evidence through assignments, exams, projects and surveys, then review it at course or programme level. The cycle repeats, with outcomes revised when the evidence shows they are unclear, unmeasurable or simply not being reached.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on student data, which is protected by institutional policy and, in many jurisdictions, by privacy law, so grades, submissions and analytics need clear handling rules. Accessibility obligations shape how outcomes are written and how assessments are delivered, and accommodation requests have to be planned for rather than improvised. Provenance matters for shared rubrics and syllabus content, since reuse across courses should respect the terms under which the material was created. Accreditation bodies and internal review committees are the usual authorities that audit whether stated outcomes are actually assessed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward outcomes that name durable capabilities, such as evaluating sources or working with AI tools, rather than tool-specific skills that date quickly. Programmes are moving from annual review to continuous evidence gathering, using data already produced by normal coursework. Interest is growing in making outcomes legible to students, so they can see how a task connects to a capability they will carry out of the course. The open question is how much of assessment can be automated without losing the judgement that makes a credential trustworthy.
